sample.universe: Denmark. Three distinct empirical exhibits: (i) the aggregate national unemployment rate 1980-2020; (ii) young Danish workers observed monthly in payroll records for two years before and after their 18th birthday; (iii) newly unemployed recipients of unemployment insurance in two Danish counties enrolled in the Quickly Back to Work randomized experiment in the winter of 2005-2006.
sample.unit_of_observation: varies by exhibit: country-year (Figure 1), person-month of age (Figure 2), person-week of unemployment duration (Figure 4)
selection_rules: Figure 1: people in the labor force registered as unemployed in administrative records, including participants in active labor market programs, 1980-2020; the dashed lines are averages for 1980-1994 and 2006-2020
Figure 2: young workers aged 16-20, restricted to the 24 months before and the 24 months after the 18th birthday

Figure 4: "All individuals in the two counties who became unemployed, and who were entitled to unemployment insurance benefits during this period"; "those born on the 1st to the 15th were given the treatment, and those born on the 16th to the 31st were not"

construction_notes: Figure 1 plots "the share of people in the labor force who are unemployed", based on administrative records of registered unemployed and including participants in active labor market programs; the two gray dashed lines are period averages for 1980-1994 (printed 10.4%) and 2006-2020 (printed 4.4%).
Percentage changes at the age-18 discontinuity (the 33 percent employment drop and the 40 percent wage jump) "are computed using the midpoint method" (Figure 2 note, p. 10).

Figure 2 "replicates Figure 1.B in Kreiner et al. (2020), which describes the data and the estimation of the fitted line and the percentage drop in employment at age 18"; the estimation itself is not described in this paper.

Figure 4 "partly replicates Figure 4 of Gautier et al. (2018a)" and shows raw survivor functions (fraction still unemployed) by elapsed duration in weeks for the randomly assigned treatment and control groups.
No estimating equation, standard error, confidence interval or p-value is printed anywhere in the paper; Table 1 is a table of OECD levels and ranks, not a regression table.
Table 1 indicators are OECD levels and ranks among 36 OECD countries, with (+)/(-) marking the direction in which higher values are ranked better or worse.

claims.statement: The intensified Danish active labor market policy introduced with the 1994 "rights and duties" reform (alongside the changes in the unemployment insurance scheme) lowered the long-run Danish unemployment rate, which fell from an average of 10.4 percent in 1980-1994 to 4.4 percent in 2006-2020.

treatment.label: the revised flexicurity regime: the intensified Danish active labor market policy with compulsory participation ("rights and duties"), introduced by the major labor market reform of 1994

register_source.value: Ministry of Employment (1993-2019) for program participation shares; no register code or variable named

definition.value: A regime shift rather than an individual-level treatment: the 1994 reform required recipients of unemployment insurance and of social assistance to apply for jobs, to participate in active labor market policies and to accept job offers fitting their profiles, with benefit sanctions for non-compliance, and sharply raised program intensity - from one in six unemployed participating in a program during the year in 1993-1994 to more than half of the unemployed participating annually in the last decade. Maximum unemployment insurance duration was also cut (to four years around 2000 and then to two years).

timing.value: introduced in 1994; the post-reform comparison period used in Figure 1 is 2006-2020, the pre-reform period 1980-1994

outcome.label: unemployment rate in Denmark (percent of the labor force)

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark (1980-2020): administrative records of people registered as unemployed, including participants in active labor market programs; no register code or variable named

definition.value: "the share of people in the labor force who are unemployed. It is based on administrative records of people who are registered as unemployed and includes people who participate in active labor market programs" (Figure 1 note); the quantity compared is the long-run (period) average of this annual rate.

units.value: percentage points (difference between the 2006-2020 and the 1980-1994 average unemployment rate)

magnitude.interpretation: "the revised flexicurity regime was followed by a descent of the unemployment rate over the next 15 years to a much lower long-run level"; the authors call it a "major improvement in labor market performance".

estimand.target_population: Denmark as a whole: the long-run (period-average) national unemployment rate under the old versus the new flexicurity regime
estimand.time_horizon: long-run averages: 1980-1994 under the old regime versus 2006-2020 under the new regime, i.e. roughly 12 to 26 years after the 1994 reform

population.description: Denmark: all people in the labor force; the national registered unemployment rate 1980-2020
population.selection: national aggregate from administrative records of people registered as unemployed, including participants in active labor market programs

identification.source_of_variation: The 1994 Danish labor market reform that introduced the "rights and duties" principle and the subsequent intensification of active labor market programs; the evidence is a before/after comparison of long-run average unemployment (1980-1994 versus 2006-2020) in a single aggregate time series, with no control group and no regression.

key_assumptions.assumption: The fall in the long-run unemployment rate after the early 1990s is attributable mainly to the intensified active labor market policy (together with the unemployment insurance changes) rather than to other developments occurring over the same four decades.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No formal test. The authors argue against two alternatives: decentralization of wage bargaining ("The organizational changes seem too small to fully explain the big decline in unemployment", p. 9-10) and the earned income tax credit (introduced in Denmark only in 2004, footnote 6, p. 8).

key_assumptions.assumption: The 1990s decentralization of Danish wage setting is too small a change to explain the decline in unemployment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Authors' assessment only; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: An earned income tax credit cannot explain the drop in unemployment, because it was implemented in Denmark only in 2004, after the drop took place.

threats_discussed: decentralization of wage bargaining during the 1990s and the resulting rise in wage dispersion as an alternative explanation
the earned income tax credit (implemented in Denmark in 2004) as an alternative explanation
concurrent changes in the unemployment insurance scheme: shorter maximum benefit duration and targeted replacement-rate reductions, e.g. for workers under 25
the possibility that the collective bargaining system itself (efficient bargaining, wage compression) explains Danish labor market performance
unresolved_confounders: changes in the unemployment insurance scheme occurred at the same time; the authors attribute the improvement "mainly" - not solely - to the active labor market policy
business-cycle composition of the 1980-1994 and 2006-2020 averages is not addressed
no control group, counterfactual or statistical test is reported for the regime comparison

estimator.value: comparison of period averages of an aggregate annual time series (dashed long-run averages plotted in Figure 1); no regression, standard error or test is reported

source_table.value: Figure 1, p. 7 (printed averages 10.4% for 1980-1994 and 4.4% for 2006-2020); discussed on pp. 7-8

mediators_claimed: screening out of applicants who are not involuntarily unemployed (workfare as a screening device against adverse selection)
threat/motivation effect: more intensive job search and lower reservation wages to avoid program participation
moderated wage claims of workers and unions through a worsened outside option
higher worker productivity and reduced information frictions from program participation

heterogeneity.finding: "the effects do vary considerably across program characteristics and targeted groups"; experiments targeted at unemployed with weak labor market attachment (long-term social assistance recipients, people on sickness benefits, young unemployed with mental or cognitive challenges) gave less positive results and a subset of programs did not meet cost-effectiveness requirements (p. 16)

nodes: intensified active labor market policy with rights and duties (1994 reform)

edges.from: intensified active labor market policy with rights and duties (1994 reform)

ambiguities: Figure 1 prints 10.4% and 4.4% for the two regime averages; the -6.0 percentage-point gap is our subtraction, not a number the paper prints.

The paper reports no control group, standard error or test for this comparison, so statistically_significant is left null and identification is recorded as descriptive even though the paper words the claim causally ("We attribute ...").
The treatment bundles the active labor market policy intensification with the contemporaneous unemployment insurance reforms; the authors say "mainly" the former.

evidence.annotation: Figure 1 Unemployment Rate in Denmark | in-plot labels: "10.4%" (left dashed line) and "4.4%" (right dashed line); y-axis "Percent"; x-axis 1980 to 2020 | "Source: Statistics Denmark (1980–2020)." | "Notes: The graph plots the share of people in the labor force who are unemployed. It is based on administrative records of people who are registered as unemployed and includes people who participate in active labor market programs. The gray dashed lines are averages for 1980–1994 and 2006–2020."

evidence.how: 4.4 - 10.4 = -6.0 percentage points, using the two long-run averages printed on Figure 1 (10.4% for 1980-1994 and 4.4% for 2006-2020); the paper itself prints only the two levels, never the difference.

value.claimed_domain: Denmark; the authors explicitly question whether a flexicurity policy of this kind is feasible or desirable for the United States
boundary_conditions: massive public spending on active labor market policy (about 2 percent of GDP in Denmark versus 0.1 percent in the United States), and maybe also on education in general, is "a necessary condition"
a small and very homogeneous population receiving more or less the same basic public education
a substantial number of caseworkers with a high level of government information about individuals
prevailing social attitudes: trust in government, civic-mindedness, and perceiving the jobless as unlucky rather than lazy

theory_referenced: workfare as a screening device against adverse selection in unemployment compensation (Hansen and Tranaes 1999; Kreiner and Tranaes 2005)
equilibrium search model in which workfare mitigates moral hazard in job search and wage formation (Andersen and Svarer 2014)

anchor_quote.text: We attribute this major improvement in labor market performance mainly to the intensified Danish active labor market policy, alongside the changes in the unemployment insurance scheme.

claims.statement: At the age-18 discontinuity in the negotiated minimum wage, employment of young Danish workers drops by 15 percentage points (one-third of the employed), showing that Danish firms do not keep low-skilled workers whose wage costs exceed their productivity.

treatment.label: turning 18 years old, and thereby becoming eligible for the significantly higher negotiated adult minimum wage

register_source.value: monthly payroll records for the Danish population (via Kreiner et al. 2020); no register code or variable named

definition.value: The age discontinuity in the collectively agreed minimum wage: "the basic minimum hourly wage rate of a young adult who is 18 years or older was around $15 in 2016. It is considerably lower when younger" (p. 9). The running variable is the month relative to the 18th birthday; the discontinuity is at month 0.

timing.value: at the 18th birthday; the window is 24 months before to 24 months after

register_source.value: monthly payroll records for the Danish population (via Kreiner et al. 2020); no register code or variable named

definition.value: "employment rates by age, in months, for two years before and after individuals turn 18 years old. It is based on monthly payroll records for the Danish population" (Figure 2 note); the drop is read off fitted lines on each side of the 18th birthday, and the percentage change is computed using the midpoint method.

timing.value: at the 18th birthday (month 0 of the running variable)

units.value: percentage points of the employment rate

magnitude.interpretation: "This implies that one-third of the employed lose their job when they turn 18 years old"; equivalently "employment drops by 15 percentage points, or 33 percent", the percentage change being computed with the midpoint method.

estimand.target_population: young Danish workers at the age-18 minimum wage discontinuity (the effect of the minimum wage hike for those turning 18)

population.description: Danish population of young workers observed in monthly payroll records, at ages 16-20, in the 24 months before and after their 18th birthday
population.ages: 16-20 (monthly age; 24 months either side of the 18th birthday)
population.selection: young workers observed in monthly payroll records for the Danish population; the paper states no further restriction

identification.source_of_variation: The discontinuous jump in the collectively negotiated minimum wage when a worker turns 18, observed at monthly frequency in population payroll records (Kreiner, Reck, and Skov 2020).

key_assumptions.assumption: Turning 18 affects employment only through the jump in the negotiated minimum wage; nothing else that affects employment changes discontinuously at the 18th birthday.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here. The paper notes that the observed wage jump of 40 percent "is of a similar size as the jump in the agreed minimum wage levels", so that "minimum wages appear to be binding".

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the minimum wage increase, employment would have evolved smoothly in age through the 18th birthday (continuity of counterfactual mean employment at the cutoff).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 2 shows monthly employment profiles on both sides of the cutoff with fitted lines; the estimation of the fitted line is described in Kreiner et al. (2020), not in this paper.

key_assumptions.assumption: The negotiated minimum wage is binding for young workers, so the agreed wage floor determines their wage.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The observed wage jump at 18 is of similar size to the jump in the agreed minimum wage levels (p. 9).

threats_discussed: the alternative hypothesis that workers and firms agree on wage compression, so that less-skilled people are paid above their productivity and employment is not on the labor demand curve - the hypothesis this figure is used to reject

estimator.value: graphical regression discontinuity: monthly employment rates by month of age with a fitted line on each side of the 18th birthday; percentage change computed with the midpoint method. The estimation of the fitted line and of the percentage drop is described in Kreiner et al. (2020), not in this paper.

source_table.value: Figure 2, p. 10 (employment rate around workers' 18th birthday); discussed on p. 9

mediators_claimed: the jump in the negotiated adult minimum wage, which pushes wage costs above the productivity of some young workers
ambiguities: The figure is a replication of Figure 1.B in Kreiner et al. (2020) (Kreiner being an author of both); the estimation is described there, not here, so the design details recorded are the ones this paper states.
The paper names no estimand; we record ATE at the cutoff.
No pre-period employment level is printed, so baseline_mean is null; the 33 percent figure is a midpoint-method percentage and cannot be inverted to a baseline mean.

claims.statement: In the Danish Quickly Back to Work randomized experiment, the share of newly unemployed still unemployed after ten weeks is about 10 percentage points lower in the treatment group (about 50 percent) than in the control group (around 60 percent), a reduction of 15 percent.

treatment.label: Quickly Back to Work treatment: intensified active labor market measures for newly unemployed UI recipients

register_source.value: weekly unemployment data for the two groups of unemployed (Gautier et al. 2018b); no register code or variable named

definition.value: "intensified labor market measures, involving information, early mandatory participation in job search assistance programs, frequent meetings with case workers, and full-time program participation in an active labor market program for at least three months for those still unemployed after 18 weeks" (p. 14). The control group "was subject to the traditional labor market policy" (Figure 4 note).

timing.value: from entry into unemployment, winter 2005-2006, in two Danish counties

outcome.label: share still unemployed after ten weeks (fraction of individuals still unemployed at an elapsed unemployment duration of 10 weeks)

register_source.value: weekly unemployment data for the two groups of unemployed (Gautier et al. 2018b); no register code or variable named

definition.value: "the fraction of individuals that are still unemployed at different elapsed durations of unemployment" (Figure 4 note) - the empirical survivor function in unemployment, read at 10 weeks of elapsed duration, in percent.

timing.value: ten weeks after entry into unemployment

units.value: percentage points (treatment minus control share still unemployed after ten weeks)

magnitude.interpretation: "The 10 percentage-points lower unemployment rate in the treatment group corresponds to a reduction of 15 percent."

estimand.target_population: newly unemployed individuals entitled to unemployment insurance benefits in the two Danish counties covered by the experiment in the winter of 2005-2006
estimand.time_horizon: after ten weeks of elapsed unemployment duration

population.description: All individuals in two Danish counties who became unemployed and were entitled to unemployment insurance benefits during the winter of 2005-2006, allocated to a treatment or a control group
subgroups_defined: treatment group (born on the 1st to the 15th of a month)
control group (born on the 16th to the 31st of a month)
population.selection: newly unemployed recipients of unemployment insurance in the two experimental counties during the experiment window; assignment by day of birth

identification.source_of_variation: Random allocation to treatment and control in the Quickly Back to Work ("Hurtigt i gang") experiment organized by the Danish Ministry of Labor: "those born on the 1st to the 15th were given the treatment, and those born on the 16th to the 31st were not", among all newly unemployed UI-entitled individuals in two counties in the winter of 2005-2006.

key_assumptions.assumption: Allocation by day of birth is random, so treatment status is independent of the unobserved determinants of unemployment duration.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The design: all newly unemployed UI-entitled individuals in the two counties were allocated to treatment or control by day of birth (p. 14). No balance table is reported in this paper.

claims.statement: The employment loss at the age-18 minimum wage hike is temporary in level terms: it takes two additional years, until age 20, before the employment rate is back to the level it had before the wage hike, so by 24 months after the 18th birthday no employment shortfall remains.

key_assumptions.assumption: The pre-18 employment level is the right benchmark for the post-18 employment path, i.e. employment would otherwise have been flat in age over this window.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing beyond the visual comparison of the Figure 2 profile with its pre-18 level; employment generally rises with age in this age range, which the paper does not address.

unresolved_confounders: the recovery is a return to the pre-18 level, not an estimate of the counterfactual employment path at age 20; the paper gives no counterfactual for that horizon

estimator.value: visual reading of the monthly employment profile in Figure 2: the number of months after the 18th birthday at which employment returns to its pre-18 level; no estimate, standard error or test reported

mediators_claimed: firms' quick employment adjustment to the higher wage cost, followed by re-absorption of the cohort as productivity and experience rise with age
ambiguities: The paper prints no estimate, standard error or test for the +24-month horizon; the null is the stated return of employment to its pre-hike level, read off Figure 2.

A return to the pre-18 LEVEL is not the same as a zero treatment effect at age 20, since employment would normally rise with age; the paper does not make that distinction, and we record the claim as the paper states it.
